buyer_reported_costs.finding: A law firm owner says he was paying between $1,000 and $2,500 a month for a human answering service before switching to an AI receptionist.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Testimonial on Upfirst's pricing page from attorney Thomas Davenport; reported spend on the prior service, not the AI price

buyer_reported_costs.finding: A nonprofit program director says the next human answering option was $400 a month.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Upfirst testimonial from AFL-CIO Community Services; used to justify the AI plan

buyer_reported_costs.finding: A five-office dental group's AI receptionist cost $8,554 for one month while handling 573 calls and booking $66,342 in production.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Vendor-published ROI case study for Fortify's 'Lucy' AI receptionist; cost is for five locations combined, so it is not a single-location list price

buyer_reported_costs.finding: Small-business posters cite AI receptionist plans around $29-$199 a month, with custom or more managed setups around $500 a month or more.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Reddit threads on AI receptionist pricing; individual anecdotes and some vendor pitches, not verified invoices

buyer_reported_costs.finding: One user reported being asked nearly $60 a month just to keep access to calls/voicemail after a free-tier change; another reported waiting nine months for a promised refund.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Third-party analysis of 55 user reports (Reddit, Trustpilot, App Store) about AI receptionists; reported complaints, not verified invoices

buyer_reported_costs.finding: A managed IT provider says one client cut call handling from $4,500 a month with a human receptionist service to under $500 a month with an AI receptionist.
buyer_reported_costs.context: Vendor case study by Seashore IT (Western US, not New Jersey); the $500 figure is a client total, not a published list price

what_is_included_vs_extra.point: Human escalation is bundled at Smith.ai but not at Goodcall: Smith routes complex calls to a live North America-based receptionist 24/7, while a third-party review notes Goodcall has no human backup and transfers only to the client's own staff.
Calendar booking and warm/live transfers are not on Rosie's $49 entry plan; they start on the $149 plan, so a usable booking receptionist costs three times the headline price.

Dialzara bills phone numbers separately ($3/month US local, $5/month US toll-free), plus $19/month + $0.05 per AI message for SMS and $39/month standalone for website chat; custom prompt engineering is only included on Elite or the $1,500+ Done for You tier.

Upfirst includes CRM API/Zapier and calendar booking on every plan, but team-done integration setup, white-glove onboarding and priority support only on Scale/Enterprise; each extra agent costs $9.95/month.
Goodcall's tiers limit external tools (1/5/15), team members (1/5/10), workers (5/20) and AI test runs; top-ups cost $5 at a time and Starter keeps only 30 days of call history.
My AI Front Desk includes 200 voice minutes, but extra minutes draw on a 1,000-credit pool (25 credits = $0.25 per minute) that expires monthly; out-of-pool auto-reload is 1,000 credits for $10.

Sarah 24/7 includes white-glove setup, porting, calendar/CRM connections, after-hours and Spanish at no extra charge, and charges the same 35¢/minute with no penalty tier; a second channel is $100/month.
Fusion Calling includes all integrations even on Starter, but adds one-time setup of $799 on Pro and $1,250 on Enterprise for configuration, integration setup, testing and launch support.
ZAVYANS quotes a management retainer but bills AI platform usage (call minutes/messages) separately at cost, so the advertised monthly price is not the all-in cost.
Lithium's $179 managed plan includes setup, call rules, calendar/CRM hooks and testing, but publishes no minute allowance or overage rate, so usage risk is undisclosed.
Slang.ai bundles reservation-platform integrations and bilingual support at Core, but custom workflows, custom integrations, reporting and SSO only at Enterprise.

buyer_complaints.complaint: Callers hang up on the AI and the business never finds out; because no message or transcript is created, the lost lead leaves no trace.
Agents loop, repeat themselves or misunderstand accents and off-script requests instead of handing off to a person.
Usage-based billing surprises: short calls billed like long ones, credit tiers, and unclear overage rules are the most common pricing complaints.
Booking errors, including wrong service booked or double-booked jobs, create more work than the AI saves.
The sales demo is smoother than the real deployment, and some buyers report aggressive upsell pitches during onboarding.
Goodcall has no human receptionist backup, its entry plan keeps call details for only 30 days (a third-party review reported 7 days), and scheduling/CRM depth is not stated on the pricing page.
Dialzara's $29 plan includes only 60 minutes, so modest call volume pushes buyers into overage; a third-party review also flags at least one one-star complaint about support being hard to reach.
Per-call billing irritates some law-firm buyers, who describe it as sketchy or steep at $7-$9 per call; they prefer predictable billing.

price_ranges.low_cost_self_serve: $0-$99/month entry plans; typically 25-250 calls or 60-220 minutes included
price_ranges.full_service_or_custom: $350-$1,500+/month, plus $499-$1,999 one-time setup at managed agencies
price_ranges.inference_note: Ranges are the low and high published list prices observed on vendor pages on 2026-11-12, grouped by what the plan includes, not averages or quotes. Entry plans cluster under $99 but carry thin allowances (25-250 calls or 60-220 minutes). Usable small-business plans with booking and transfers cluster at $99-$350. Managed/done-for-you offers with setup, tuning and human escalation start around $350-$1,500+, and setup fees of $499-$1,999 appear at agencies. Usage overages and add-ons (numbers, SMS, extra agents, extra channels) sit on top and are excluded from the ranges.

implications_for_consultancy: Inference: the consultancy should compete in the $179-$599/month managed band, not the $29-$99 self-serve band. Reasoning: local NJ/NY-area managed offers publish $179 (Lithium), $299-$599 (UpNewLevel) and $350 + 35¢/min (Sarah 24/7), while self-serve tools at $29-$99 leave the buyer to configure prompts, calendars and escalation themselves. A local consultancy's labour is the product, so it should be priced against managed providers.

Inference: a one-time setup fee of $500-$1,500 is defensible and already normalized. Reasoning: ZAVYANS publishes $499/$999/$1,999 setup, Fusion Calling $799/$1,250, and a third-party setup-fee guide describes $500-$1,000 as typical. Charging $0 setup to win on price would undervalue integration and testing work that buyers already pay agencies for.

Inference: the strongest recurring price points are roughly $249-$349 for a single-location 5-20 staff client and $449-$799 for multi-location or CRM-heavy clients. Reasoning: these bracket the published managed plans (Lithium $179, UpNewLevel $299, Sarah $350, ZAVYANS $249-$799) and sit below the $1,000-$2,500 that some buyers report paying human answering services.

Inference: a pilot priced at $500-$1,500 including setup, 30 days of tuning and a written escalation plan is likely to convert because it is smaller than the annual commitment implied by a $299-$599 monthly plan and matches the low end of observed setup fees. Reasoning: buyers' biggest reported fear is billing surprises and demo-vs-reality gaps, so a fixed-scope paid pilot answers that objection directly.

Inference: include human escalation, after-hours rules, bilingual handling and transcript review in the base retainer rather than selling them as add-ons. Reasoning: these are exactly where cheap self-serve deployments fail in buyer reports (hangups, loops, missed emergencies), and local managed competitors already bundle setup, Spanish and changes.

Inference: avoid per-call pricing and publish a clear included-minute allowance with a capped overage. Reasoning: per-call billing draws complaints from law firms, and the most common complaint pattern across 55 reports is usage/credit billing shock; a flat or capped plan is easier to sell against Smith.ai's per-call model and My AI Front Desk's expiring credit pool.

Inference: the consultancy's margin comes from configuration and ongoing tuning, not from reselling minutes. Reasoning: underlying platform costs are visible ($29-$350/month plus $0.20-$0.48/min overage, or white-label programs at Dialzara and Fusion Calling), so clients can benchmark the software component; the defensible charge is for integration, testing, call-review and accountability.

Inference: offer annual prepay at about 10-15% off rather than matching '2 months free'. Reasoning: Rosie and several competitors advertise two months free (about 17%), but a local practice with hands-on onboarding has real first-year labour and should not fund the full discount; a smaller annual incentive still matches the market's annual-billing expectation.
caveats: All vendor list prices were read on 2026-11-12. Prices on these pages change frequently and several pages render tiers by script, so the retrieved figure may differ from a later visit.

Smith.ai's 150-call Pro price ($270/mo) is produced by the page's call-volume selector; it was confirmed through a search result quoting the vendor page rather than static page text. The 300-call Enterprise total ($500/mo) is static; the 500-call and 1,000+ options are shown only as per-call rates or 'custom'.

Rosie's page renders the plan labels out of price order (Professional $49, Scale $149, Growth $299). Tier names are reported as the vendor's schema and page show them; buyers should confirm at checkout.
Rosie publishes no voice overage rate; the automatic-upgrade-to-next-plan behavior comes from a third-party source and was not confirmed in Rosie's public terms, which only discuss SMS overage.

Goodcall's live page (checked 2026-11-12) shows Scale at $299 for 2,000 unique customers and $0.15 overage. A third-party review dated 2026-09-07 lists Scale at $249 for 500 customers and $0.50 overage, and annual prices of $66/$108/$208. Those figures conflict with the live page and were not used.

Slang.ai's $399/$599 starting prices appear in the page source for the USD version; the rendered page shows feature lists and a 'Get a quote' button. The same page geo-switches to CAD and AUD, so only the USD figures are used.

Several vendors do not publish usage allowances or overage rates (Lithium, UpNewLevel, Slang.ai), and others do not publish annual totals (Rosie, Goodcall). 'Not published' is recorded rather than estimated.
Buyer-reported figures are anecdotes or vendor case studies, not audited invoices. Case-study costs may cover multiple locations and are labeled as such.
G2, Capterra and Trustpilot blocked automated access during this research, so review evidence is drawn from accessible third-party analyses and vendor pages rather than the review sites' full text.

Numa (the dealership AI phone agent named in the brief) publishes no price; its FAQ says pricing is per plan and confirmed on a demo. It is therefore excluded from the offerings list and noted in data_gaps.
data_gaps: Numa: no public price. Vendor FAQ says plans are scaled to team size and systems and priced after a demo; a third-party estimate of about $199/month per location is unconfirmed and was not used.
Smith.ai's exact monthly totals for its 300-call Pro option, 500-call Enterprise option and 1,000+ custom option are not shown as static prices.
Rosie's exact annual-billing totals (as opposed to '2 months free') are not displayed on the page.
Goodcall's annual pricing and any contract/cancellation specifics beyond month-to-month are not stated on its pricing page.
Slang.ai's contract length, setup fee, included call/minutes volume and overage rate are not published.
Lithium and UpNewLevel do not publish included minutes, overage rates or usage caps, so their all-in cost at high call volume cannot be compared.

No New Jersey-specific survey or invoice dataset of what 5-200 staff businesses actually pay for AI receptionists was found; local evidence is limited to provider list prices and national buyer anecdotes.
Simple Phones (from $97/month for 100 calls) and other small self-serve vendors were reviewed but excluded to keep the vendor set at 12; their higher tiers are not public.
No reliable public data on AI receptionist churn, renewal rates or realized savings for Middlesex County businesses was found.
